title: Best Laptop for Computer Science Students 2026 | ComputingForGeeks
text:
## Best laptop for computer science students: the quick picks

If you only read one section, read this one. Each pick has a verdict and the reason it beat the others in its slot:

- Best overall: Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 16 (Ryzen AI 7 445, 16GB, 512GB). Two SO-DIMM slots and two M.2 slots for about $960, so you can grow it to 32GB later instead of paying RAM-crunch prices now.
- Best MacBook: MacBook Air 13 (M5, 16GB, 512GB). Fanless, rated for up to 15 hours of web use and about $1,150 on Amazon, but the 16GB is soldered for good.
- Best budget: Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3 15 (Core 5 210H, 16GB, 512GB). An 8-core Intel laptop with the 16GB that WSL 2 and Docker need for about $600, with a dim screen as the price you pay.
- Best for machine learning and game development: Lenovo LOQ 15 (Ryzen 7 250, RTX 5060 8GB). CUDA on a real NVIDIA GPU for about $1,250, two RAM slots and Ethernet, but it weighs 2.1 kg.

Prices here are what the Amazon listings showed when we checked, and laptop prices move weekly in 2026. Black Friday and the run-up to the January semester are when most students buy, so it’s worth watching the live price for a week or two before you commit.

...

| Laptop | CPU | RAM as sold | Upgrade path | Storage | Weight | Approx. price |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| IdeaPad Slim 5 16 (16AGP11) | Ryzen AI 7 445, 6C/12T | 16GB DDR5-5600 | 2 SO-DIMM slots, 32GB listed max | 512GB, 2 M.2 slots | 1.75 to 1.85 kg | about $960 |
| MacBook Air 13 (M5) | M5, 10 cores | 16GB unified | None, soldered | 512GB, soldered | 1.23 kg | about $1,150 |
| IdeaPad Slim 3 15 (15IRH10R) | Core 5 210H, 8C/12T | 16GB DDR5-4800 | 8GB soldered + 1 SO-DIMM (filled), 24GB max | 512GB, 2 M.2 2242 slots | from 1.59 kg | about $600 |
| LOQ 15 (15AHP11) | Ryzen 7 250, 8C/16T | 16GB DDR5-5600 | 2 SO-DIMM slots, 32GB listed max | 512GB, 2 M.2 slots | from 2.1 kg | about $1,250 |

...

## 1. Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 16 (Ryzen AI 7 445)

The IdeaPad Slim 5 16 is the best overall pick because it gives you the most room to grow on both memory and storage for under $1,000. It’s the 2026 model (16AGP11), sold and shipped by Amazon in Luna Grey with 16GB and a 512GB SSD:

Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5 16 (16AGP11): two DDR5 SO-DIMM slots and two M.2 slots. Shown in blue; the linked listing is Luna Grey. Image: Lenovo.

Lenovo’s PSREF datasheet lists two DDR5-5600 SO-DIMM slots with nothing soldered, and two M.2 slots (a 2242 and a 2280, both PCIe 4.0) with one SSD fitted. That layout matters more than the CPU. That second slot lets you add an SSD for Linux and dual boot alongside Windows without touching the Windows drive. Lenovo lists 32GB as the maximum it offers, which you can reach by swapping modules once memory prices cool.

The Ryzen AI 7 445 is a 6-core, 12-thread chip with Radeon 840M graphics. Given that our whole course stack peaked at 2.1GB, that’s enough CPU and memory for coursework under WSL 2 with Docker, but it is not the pick for heavy parallel builds. The ports cover a student’s week:

- Two USB-C at 10Gbps: both charge and drive a display, so one cable docks it in the library.
- Two USB-A and HDMI 2.1: no dongle for a projector or a lab-room mouse.
- microSD reader: handy for Raspberry Pi courses.

Where it falls short: there is no Thunderbolt and no Ethernet port, and the battery is 50, 60 or 80Wh depending on the configuration, with the Amazon listing not saying which. We also found no Ubuntu certification for this model, so treat Linux as likely but untested on our side. Pick it if you’re on Windows with WSL 2 and want one laptop that can still grow in your third year; look elsewhere when MacBook-class battery life matters most. It was about $960 when we checked, so check the live price.

## 2. MacBook Air 13 (M5)

The MacBook Air 13 is the best pick if your course doesn’t mandate Windows and you value battery life and silence over upgradability. The M5 model with 16GB of unified memory and a 512GB SSD was about $1,150 on Amazon when we checked, which beat Apple’s own education price:

MacBook Air 13 (M5): 16GB unified memory, 53.8Wh battery, 1.23 kg and fanless. Image: Apple.

The RAM crunch hit Apple too. Apple raised this configuration from $1,099 to $1,299 in June 2026, and the Apple Education Store takes $100 off that for students, to $1,199. Amazon’s $1,149 was lower than both on the day we checked, which will not always hold, so compare the two before you order.

For a CS student, the case for the Air is the battery and the Unix shell. Apple rates the 53.8Wh battery at up to 15 hours of web use, and the laptop weighs 1.23 kg with no fan. macOS gives you zsh, Homebrew and a POSIX userland without WSL in the middle, and Docker Desktop is free for education use under Docker’s licence terms. The costs are real, though:

- Memory and SSD are soldered: the 16GB and 512GB you buy are what you graduate with.
- Docker images are arm64 first: amd64-only course images run under emulation, slower than native, and Docker’s Rosetta option is off by default.
- Linux runs in a VM or containers: plan on that rather than installing Linux on the laptop itself.
- Two Thunderbolt ports and MagSafe only: HDMI and USB-A need a hub.

Notebookcheck also found the fanless M5 throttles after a couple of minutes of sustained multi-core load, which you’ll notice on long builds but not on coursework. Pick the Air if your school is Mac-friendly and you want the laptop that lasts a full day of lectures; avoid it when a course needs x86 Windows tools or you expect to need more than 16GB. The 24GB configuration costs more, so price it against the Slim 5 plus a later upgrade.

## 3. Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3 15 (Core 5 210H)

The IdeaPad Slim 3 15 is the budget pick because it gets the things that matter right at about $600: 16GB, a 512GB SSD and an 8-core Intel CPU that runs WSL 2 and Docker without complaint. This listing is the 15IRH10R (83K40054US), sold by Electronic Express rather than Amazon itself:

Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3 15 (15IRH10R): Core 5 210H, 16GB, two M.2 2242 slots, from 1.59 kg. Image: Lenovo.

The Core 5 210H has 8 cores (4 performance, 4 efficient) and 12 threads, more cores than the Slim 5’s Ryzen. The compromises are elsewhere. PSREF says the 15.3-inch WUXGA panel is 300 nits with 45% NTSC coverage, so it is dim and washed out next to the MacBook, and the ports are basic: one 5Gbps USB-C, two USB-A, HDMI 1.4 and an SD reader.

Memory is the catch to know before you buy. PSREF lists 8GB soldered to the board plus one DDR5 SO-DIMM slot, with 24GB as the maximum Lenovo offers. On this 16GB model that slot already holds an 8GB module, so there is no free slot, and the only upgrade is swapping that module for a 16GB one to reach 24GB. We’d still take it over any 8GB laptop at the same price, because 16GB covers the whole course stack we measured. Pick it if your budget stops around $600 and you’ll live with the screen; pass on it when you already know a course needs 32GB. Check the live price before you order.

...

The LOQ 15 is the pick for students heading into machine learning, computer vision or game development, because it is the only laptop here with an NVIDIA GPU, and most ML coursework assumes CUDA. The 2026 model (15AHP11) with a Ryzen 7 250, an RTX 5060 and 16GB was about $1,250 from antonline when we checked:

...

- IdeaPad Slim 5 16: no Thunderbolt, no Ethernet, and a battery size the listing doesn’t state.
- MacBook Air 13 (M5): 16GB and 512GB forever, amd64 containers under emulation, and a hub for HDMI.
- IdeaPad Slim 3 15: a dim 300-nit screen and no free RAM slot, with 24GB as the ceiling by swapping the one module.
- LOQ 15: 2.1 kg

...

For most students on a Windows course, we’d buy the Slim 5 at 16GB and add memory in year two or three when prices fall back. Choose the MacBook Air if your school is Mac-friendly and battery life wins, and save the LOQ for the students who know CUDA is coming. If you’re already working as a developer rather than studying, our best laptops for programming guide aims higher.

title: Best Laptop for Computer Science Students Under $1,000 (2026)
text:
## The short answer

| Pick | Best for | Price right now | Why it’s here |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lenovo ThinkPad E14 Gen 7 (AMD) | Overall — the four-year machine | $780–$900 | Two real RAM slots and a spare SSD bay. It’s the only one you can fix later. |
| Dell 14 Plus (DB14250) | Screen and battery, zero compatibility drama | $949–$995 | 2.5K 16:10 panel, Thunderbolt 4, and every x86 tool just runs. |
| Lenovo LOQ 15 (RTX 5060) | Machine learning, graphics, game dev | $799–$999 | 8GB of VRAM at a full 115 watts. Cheapest legitimate CUDA box there is. |
| HP OmniBook 5 14 | Battery life above all else | $899 | Three labs measured 25 to 32 hours. Read the ARM section first. |
| Apple MacBook Neo | Cheapest real macOS machine | $699 | Genuinely brilliant for $699. Also 8GB of RAM, permanently. |

If you take one thing from this article: buy memory, not megahertz. A 2019 laptop with 32GB is a nicer place to write code today than a 2026 laptop with 8GB. That’s not a hot take, it’s just what happens when Docker Desktop opens.

...

Over four years you’ll be asked to run three or four Docker containers while your IDE indexes a few hundred files in the background. You’ll spin up a Linux VM for your operating systems course and then deliberately break it. You’ll compile something genuinely large — an LLVM pass, a Rust workspace, a kernel — while a deadline ticks. You’ll boot an Android emulator, which is a virtual machine, on top of an IDE that’s already eaten 4GB before you’ve typed a character. And you’ll do a decent chunk of this in a lecture hall where every outlet within four rows was claimed twenty minutes before you arrived.

That’s the job. Three things determine whether a laptop can hold it down:

Memory, and whether you can add more later. This is the whole ballgame. 16GB is the 2026 floor and 32GB is where you want to be if containers or VMs are on your syllabus. Almost every thin-and-light sold today solders the RAM to the board, which means whatever you buy on day one is what you’re stuck with on graduation day.

Sustained performance, not burst performance. Every chip looks fast in a ten-second benchmark. ... Thicker ones with real fans don’t.

...

### 1. Lenovo ThinkPad E14 Gen 7 (AMD) — the one I’d actually buy

Lenovo ThinkPad E14 Gen 7 (AMD)

$780–$900 for the Ryzen 7 250 / 16GB / 512GB configuration with Windows 11 Pro

This doesn’t win on any single spec. It wins because of two DDR5 SODIMM slots and an empty M.2 2280 bay.

Every other laptop in this article solders its memory down. What you buy is what you die with. The E14 lets you buy the cheap 16GB version now and, when your distributed systems course hands you a five-container Compose file in second year, drop in an $80 kit and carry on. Lenovo rates it to 64GB and there’s a second SSD slot sitting empty next to it.

...

#### My verdict

Buy the cheapest 16GB AMD configuration you can find, then upgrade the RAM yourself. Eighty dollars and fifteen minutes with a screwdriver gets you a 32GB, dual-drive-capable development machine with Windows Pro for well under $1,000 — a configuration that simply doesn’t exist as a factory option at this price.

If you want one laptop to carry you from intro data structures to your final-year capstone, this is it. Just triple-check the processor before you pay.

### 2. Dell 14 Plus (DB14250) — the best screen and the fewest surprises

Dell Pro 14 PC14250 AI Business Laptop

$949–$995 for the Core Ultra 7 258V / 32GB / 1TB configuration with the 2.5K panel

...

### 3. Lenovo LOQ 15 (RTX 5060) — the only real answer if you need CUDA

Lenovo LOQ 15.6″ Gaming Laptop

$799–$999 on sale for the Ryzen 7 250 / RTX 5060 / 16GB / 512GB configuration

If your degree contains the word “CUDA,” this is the only section that matters.

You cannot train models on integrated graphics. You cannot run Unreal Engine on a Radeon 780M. You cannot do meaningful local inference without VRAM. And a free Colab tier that disconnects at 3am mid-epoch is not a development environment, it’s a lottery.

The LOQ 15 is the cheapest honest way out of that corner.

...

### 4. HP OmniBook 5 14 — absurd battery life, one enormous caveat

HP OmniBook 5 14″ Premium Laptop

$899 for the Snapdragon X Plus X1P-42-100 / 32GB / 1TB configuration with the OLED panel

...

## Which course breaks which laptop

I’ve never seen anyone publish this, and I think it’s the most useful table here. Check it against your actual degree plan before you spend anything.

| Course | What it demands | Handles it fine | Will struggle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Intro programming, data structures | Almost nothing | All five | — |
| Web development | 8–12GB, Node, occasional containers | All five | Neo, if you go container-heavy |
| Databases | 8–16GB, Postgres or MySQL locally | E14, Dell, LOQ, OmniBook | Neo |
| Operating systems | Nested virtualisation, QEMU, 16GB+ | E14 (Hyper-V + upgradeable), Dell, LOQ | Neo, OmniBook |
| Networking | VMs, packet capture, wired ports | E14, LOQ (both have Ethernet) | Neo, OmniBook |
| Compilers | Sustained all-core load, 16GB+ | E14, LOQ | Neo (fanless throttle) |
| Machine learning | CUDA, 8GB+ VRAM | LOQ 15 only | Everything else |
| Computer graphics | Discrete GPU | LOQ 15 | Everything else |
| Android development | Emulator is a nested VM, 16GB+ | E14 (with 32GB), Dell, LOQ | Neo, OmniBook |
| iOS development | macOS required by Apple | Neo — small projects only | Every Windows machine |
| Software engineering, capstone | Docker Compose, 16–32GB | E14 upgraded, Dell 32GB | Neo, OmniBook |

...

## Where I landed

Most CS students should buy the Lenovo ThinkPad E14 Gen 7 with the AMD processor, in the cheapest 16GB configuration, and upgrade the memory themselves. That path gets you a 32GB, dual-drive-capable, Windows Pro development machine for well under $1,000, and no factory configuration at this price matches it. The screen is dim and the chip is Zen 4 in a 2026 costume. You’ll live. Just check that processor before you pay — the Lunar Lake version of the same laptop has no RAM slots at all.

If you need a GPU, the Lenovo LOQ 15 with the 115W RTX 5060 is the only real answer under $1,000, and you should buy it before Lenovo’s stock of the outgoing model runs dry in favour of the pricier, lower-power replacement. Add a second RAM stick immediately.

If you want a proper screen and long battery with zero compatibility risk, the Dell 14 Plus with the 258V, 32GB and 1TB is the polished choice. Just accept that 32GB is where it stays forever.

If your work lives in a browser and a cloud terminal, the HP OmniBook 5 14 will genuinely change how you use a laptop. Check your syllabi for Docker first, and mean it.

And if you want a Mac and you understand exactly what 8GB means, the MacBook Neo is the most laptop anyone has ever sold for $699. Go in with your eyes open and don’t be surprised in year three.

title: Back to School: The Best Budget Laptops Under $1,000
text:
## MacBook Neo

© Adriano Contreras / Gizmodo

The peppy and colorful MacBook Neo in its suite of calming colors will be a common suggestion for anybody looking for a back-to-school laptop in 2026. It starts at $700 after recent price hikes, but with a student ID you can claim it for $600. The base model comes with 256GB of storage and 8GB of unified memory. If you opt for the $800 model, you’ll double your storage to 512GB and get a Touch ID button for unlocking your laptop. If you plan on using cloud-based storage, you can feel free to opt for the cheaper model.

There’s a reason why the MacBook Neo has set the standard for budget laptops. Its all-aluminum chassis feels much more premium than its price suggests. Its screen and audio suite are also some of the best in this category. If you want a Mac that will service you for all your regular browsing, writing, or light editing tasks, this is the one you want.

## Dell XPS 13

© Dell

Dell’s direct response to the MacBook Neo tries to up the ante on visual fidelity while maintaining the solid build quality of Apple’s cheapo laptop. The Dell XPS 13 starts at $700 ($600 with a student discount), with the base version coming with 8GB of RAM and 512GB of storage (twice what you get on the MacBook Neo for the same price). It also packs in Intel’s latest Core Series 3 chips, starting with an Intel Core 5-320 CPU.

Is this going to be a powerful laptop? No, not with limited RAM and a chip that may not keep up with Apple’s designs. However, the XPS 13’s 13.4-inch display is a touchscreen and also has a variable refresh rate between 30 and 120Hz. If you want more memory, up to 16GB of RAM, you’ll need to spend $900 ($800 with the student discount).

...

For folks who imagine they need a pseudo-tablet to go along with their laptop, we can’t think of a better 2-in-1 under $1,000 than Lenovo’s Yoga 7a. This configuration has 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, as well as an AMD Ryzen AI 5 430 chip from this year.

...

© Raymond Wong / Gizmodo

As much as you may dislike the idea of ChromeOS relying on browsers to such an extent, you may not actually need anything more complicated than a Chromebook. Lenovo’s Chromebook Plus 14 is simply one of the best Chromebook Plus models around. Its MediaTek Kompanio Ultra chip, plus 16GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, is more than enough to meet the demands of whatever you plan to use a Chromebook for.

The Chromebook Plus 14 contains an OLED display that will make streaming content look rich and vibrant. Not only that, but it also has a very strong battery life that will keep up with your coursework. Just don’t expect to do too much with it. It’s still only a Chromebook.

...

If you desperately need a laptop with a discrete GPU, you’ll have a very hard time finding one new for under $1,000 in 2026. Acer’s Nitro V16 comes closest to offering an all-around budget gaming laptop with its Nvidia GeForce RTX 5050 GPU and an older AMD Ryzen 5 240 CPU. However, you still get access to 16GB of RAM and 512GB of SSD storage.

It’s also packing a 180Hz IPS LCD display that should be enough for lighter gaming or graphics tasks at the laptop’s top 1,920 x 1200 resolution. It’s not hard up for ports, either, with three USB-A, a single USB-C, plus HDMI and an Ethernet port.

At the time of writing, the Acer Nitro V16 was just under $1,000, but then it shot up to $1,059 at publishing time. Maybe you’ll get lucky and the price will drop again.
